title: More useful after death
hook: dying, Dominic promised his brothers he'd help them more from heaven

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fra Angelico's cells: a quiet fresco in every friar's room, with a Dominican standing at the edge of the Gospel scene. Your line was a painting in each cell. What image did you put in your spot? Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

Bologna, a friary, a hot summer. The founder is dying. Dominic, who by tradition walked the roads barefoot, and once talked all night with an innkeeper, is lying on the floor, by tradition on sackcloth, too weak to rise. Around him his brothers are crying. They are young, the order is young, and they don't know how they'll manage without him. What do you say to people who are about to lose you? Dominic's answer wasn't about the past. It was about the future, and he made a promise that sounds almost cheeky. Today's word is that promise.
screen: `BOLOGNA. THE FOUNDER IS DYING.` → `HIS BROTHERS ARE WEEPING.` → `LAST WORDS ABOUT THE FUTURE.`

segments.voice: An early life of Dominic, written by Jordan of Saxony, who led the order after him, tells it this way. Dominic saw his brothers weeping and told them not to. He would be more useful to them after his death, he said, than he had been in life. Read it slowly, because it's a strange comfort. Not: I'll always be in your hearts. Not: carry on my work. But: I'm not leaving the job. I'm changing posts. That rests on a Catholic belief called the communion of saints. Catholics hold that the Church is one family across death: the living on earth, the dead being made ready, and the saints with God. And family members pray for one another. So asking a saint for help is, for Catholics, like asking a friend to pray for you, only the friend is now close to God. The letter to the Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, describes believers running their race "having so great a cloud of witnesses over our head." A stadium of people who already finished, leaning over the rail. Christians don't all read this the same way. Catholic and Orthodox tradition asks the saints to pray. Some Protestant churches teach that prayer should go to God alone, and they honor the saints as examples rather than asking their help. Dominicans took Dominic at his word. Their tradition sings a short Latin antiphon to him that begins O spem miram, O wonderful hope, recalling exactly this promise to the weeping brothers. A goodbye that turned into a job description.
screen: `DON'T WEEP. I'LL BE MORE USEFUL THEN.` · `ONE FAMILY ACROSS DEATH.` · `CHURCHES READ IT DIFFERENTLY.` · `O SPEM MIRAM: O WONDERFUL HOPE.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask a saint's help, or remember someone who's gone. Settle, and breathe. If you pray to the saints, choose one, Dominic, or a saint you love, or one from this year's path, and simply ask them to pray for one thing you're carrying today. Say it plainly, the way you'd text a friend. If that isn't your practice, bring to mind someone who has died who helped you, and notice where their help is still at work in you: a habit they taught you, a phrase you still use. Stay with them. The bell holds the time.
More useful after death. Dominic's last promise to his weeping brothers: he wasn't leaving them, he was changing posts. Today's word.
Your line: more useful then. Today, when you use something a person who's gone taught you, a saying, a knot, a skill, stop and name them once. Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics ask the saints to pray for them, in private prayer and in the Church's litanies; Dominicans traditionally sing the antiphon O Spem Miram to Saint Dominic.

fork.setup: you're Dominic, dying on the floor of the friary. your young brothers are weeping. what do you tell them?
options: remember me, and carry on as best you can.
don't weep: I'll be more useful to you after death.
nothing; you're too weak to speak.
fork.reveal: Jordan of Saxony records that he told them not to weep, because he would help them more after his death than in life.

original.note: Latin: O wonderful hope. The opening of the Dominicans' antiphon to Saint Dominic, recalling his last promise.

what it means: Dominic's promise that he'd keep helping his brothers from heaven, by his prayer.
what a scholar hears: Jordan of Saxony records the promise, and the Dominican antiphon O spem miram keeps it in the order's song; it rests on the Catholic teaching of the communion of saints.

notes: Claims rule: no date of death. 'A hot summer' (August) and 'by tradition on sackcloth' / lying on the floor: confirm against Jordan of Saxony's Libellus.
The promise is paraphrased from Jordan of Saxony (no public-domain translation quoted). Confirm wording 'more useful to them after his death than in life'.
'The earliest life of Dominic' (Jordan's Libellus): a 'first/earliest' claim taken from standard Dominican historiography; confirm or soften to 'an early life'.
Communion of saints described as living, the dead being purified, and the saints in heaven; confirm phrasing 'the dead being made ready'.
Fair description of differences: Catholic and Orthodox ask saints' intercession; some Protestant churches teach prayer to God alone and honor saints as examples. Confirm.
O Spem Miram: confirm the opening words and that it recalls the deathbed promise; 'traditionally sung' in howItsDone.
